title: K–12 AI integration is lower in more disadvantaged schools while policy, training, and guidance lag adoption
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35347 national survey of K–12 school principals
geography: United States; K–12 schools and school-level AI integration

observations.period: 2026; national survey of K–12 school principals

denominator.unit: surveyed K–12 school principals; public abstract does not disclose the full respondent count

adoption_pattern.value: AI use has spread rapidly; students mainly use AI for homework help and writing, while educators use it primarily for lesson planning and administrative tasks

governance_lag.value: teacher training, guidance for student use, and school policies lagged AI adoption

disadvantage_gap.value: a one-standard-deviation increase in student disadvantage is associated with a 0.07–0.11 standard-deviation lower AI-integration index
disadvantage_gap.unit: standard deviations of school AI-integration index

school_type_gap.value: private and charter schools score 0.23–0.44 standard deviations lower than traditional public schools on the AI-integration index
school_type_gap.unit: standard deviations of school AI-integration index

district_size_explanation.value: district size accounts for roughly one-third of the disadvantage gap between public schools
district_size_explanation.unit: share of observed gap explained by district size

observations.method: National survey of K–12 school principals measuring policies, teacher training, student guidance, leadership engagement, tool availability, and AI integration; abstract reports associations and a district-size decomposition.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not disclose the full sample count, response rate, instrument details, or causal identification. The integration index is not a measure of learning, safety, teacher workload, or student welfare.
observations.subgroup: Schools by student disadvantage, sector, district size, school leaders, teachers, educators, and students.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower measured integration may reflect deliberate caution, limited appropriate use, or differences in school mission rather than a harmful access gap; more AI integration is not automatically better education.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for the working paper.
Official working-paper PDF for survey and index details.

boundary: This record measures school-level AI integration and institutional support gaps. It does not establish a causal technology-access effect, learning outcome, teacher or student wellbeing effect, privacy or safety incident, or household inequality outcome.
